item.title: MONEY ON THE RUN: the Secret Routes of the World’s Stolen Wealth
item.content:encoded: Ayele Addis Ambelu Journalist at Africa News Channel and Ethiopian Mass Media (EMMA NEWS) Media Educator at Bahir Dar University. ⓒ천지일보 The numbers read like an act of global looting: tens of billions of dollars siphoned out of fragile states every year, hidden behind shell companies, rushed through secretive commodity channels, cleaned by fast judges and polite banks in distant capitals, and, crucially, rarely returned. A fresh stocktake by the Secretariat of the African Union High-Level Panel on Illicit Financial Flows warns that the international legal and financial architecture that should stop these flows is instead a set of cracked doors and unlocked safes. The Secretariat bluntly finds that the rules, practices, and institutions that abroad jurisdictions rely on to freeze, trace, and repatriate illicit wealth systematically hamper recovery and that Africa, and many other developing regions, cannot continue to beg for crumbs when trillions in private wealth are at stake. This is a global problem, not an African parable. Global Financial Integrity’s influential estimates of trade-based illicit flows, historically used by researchers and policy makers, put the scale for developing countries in the hundreds of billions annually (earlier GFI estimates scaled at roughly $858–$1,060 billion for broader developing-country flows), a reminder that the problem is structural and transregional, not simply local theft. The AU’s own new analysis, while focused on the continent, explicitly ties African losses to patterns that happen, with variations, across Latin America, parts of Asia, and even inside advanced financial centers. How big is the leak? Different methods, different answers, and that’s the point. The AU Secretariat cites a continental annual hemorrhage in the tens of billions (it frames a plausible range used by continental analysts), and independent NGO research into one high-risk channel, artisanal gold, puts a single commodity’s annual leak at roughly the same order of magnitude. Swissaid’s 2024 field and trade-data study estimated at least $30–$35 billion of undeclared/illicit African gold exports in 2022 alone, much of it flowing through refining hubs in the UAE, Turkey, Switzerland, and India, where traceability evaporates after refining. In a single country case that reads like a razor to the national ledger, Reuters reported that Ghana alone may have lost about $11.4 billion to gold smuggling over a recent five-year span, enough to fund large chunks of national development programs or to substantially reduce sovereign borrowing. ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27. “Why should returns be treated like charity?” That indignation is not mine; it is the document’s logic. The AU Secretariat urges the UN and other global institutions to revise narrow legal definitions of “illicit” wealth to fold into the concept not only plainly criminal proceeds (embezzlement, drug profits, war-era looting) but also cross-border tax abuse, trade-misinvoicing, and aggressive profit-shifting that, while sometimes technically legal, amount to the systematic siphoning of public revenue. That conceptual shift would change the toolkit: from a reliance on slow, ad-hoc mutual legal assistance to routine, multilateral statistical monitoring, automatic sharing of beneficial-ownership data, and binding rules for fast asset freezes. In short, treat these flows as fiscal and development harms as much as criminal acts. There are voices at the top calling this what it is. United Nations institutions and global panels have repeatedly framed illicit flows as a development and security emergency: “Illicit financial flows already deprive developing countries of hundreds of billions of dollars every year,” the UN Secretariat has warned in multiple fora, and the FACTI Panel and UNODC have asked for joined-up reforms across tax, trade, and anti-money-laundering systems. The World Bank / UNODC Stolen Asset Recovery Initiative (StAR), the practitioner shop that works on the ground to pull stolen assets back, has for years highlighted how legal fragmentation and banking secrecy turn asset recovery into a trickle, not a river. The AU paper’s prescription echoes that chorus: return and reform must go hand in hand. Mechanisms of the global heist, how money leaves and why it vanishes? The playbook is now well known to anyone who studies global money flows, and the AU report lays it out with grim clarity: commercial channels (trade mis-invoicing and aggressive transfer-pricing), the informal commodity chain (artisanal minerals, timber, sometimes wildlife and fisheries), and the classic kleptocrat pathway (embezzlement routed through shell companies and luxury real estate). Each channel exploits a different legal or institutional gap: poor customs controls and weak regional border oversight for commodities; opaque corporate structures and lax country-by-country reporting for profit shifting; and secrecy jurisdictions and weak beneficial-ownership rules for kleptocratic flight. Because the beneficiaries of these systems are dispersed financiers, law firms, extraction companies, and private vaults in major cities, answering the crime requires cross-border rules that current institutions were not designed to deliver. A single case, global echoes: Ghana’s gold story. Ghana is a cautionary tale and a template. The Swissaid data and subsequent reporting show vast quantities of artisanal gold leaving West Africa under the radar, carried by passengers, misdeclared in trade reports, or routed through porous borders to hubs that absorb and refine gold beyond easy audit. Reuters’ in-depth reporting found that over recent years, Ghana lost an estimated $11.4 billion to smuggling and under-declaration — money that, in a basic arithmetic of governance, could pay for hospitals, schools, and roads. That loss is not just an accounting footnote; it weakens tax bases, increases borrowing, deepens inequality, and funds criminal and sometimes violent networks. But crucially, the route the gold takes through Dubai, Swiss vaults, and dozens of dealer networks is the same route by which other forms of wealth disappear from the books across continents. The global pattern is the same; the victims are many. Why the rich countries and financial hubs resist change and why that matters for everyone. The AU Secretariat’s stocktake is unambiguous: recovery is asymmetric. Courts and enforcement in wealthy jurisdictions sit at chokepoints. Freezing and repatriating assets requires cooperation and political will from the jurisdictions that host banks, real estate, and legal services used to hide money. That gives those jurisdictions leverage, sometimes leveraged into delay. The political economy is stark: opacity creates profit for banks and service providers, and the regulatory cost of full transparency looks like a business risk to powerful actors. This explains why international agreements remain patchy, why mutual legal assistance procedures are slow, and why Africa (and other claimants) often have to beg for cooperation instead of asserting a right enforced by a global mechanism. The AU report insists this asymmetric dependence must end: Africa must be empowered to trace and recover assets without relying on sporadic cooperation. The program for a global fix is bold, precise, and doable. The AU Secretariat and allied global panels not only diagnose, but they also provide a practical toolbox. The measures most likely to cut the leak include: automatic and reciprocal exchange of beneficial-ownership records; mandatory country-by-country corporate reporting and a clampdown on abusive transfer pricing; trade-data reconciliation programs that identify misinvoicing in near-real time; tighter controls on high-risk commodities with traceability through the supply chain; harmonized criteria for rapid asset freezes; and regional asset-recovery platforms underwritten by UN or regional institutions that speed repatriation while insulating returned funds from capture. Many of these reforms are already being piloted in bits and pieces, FACTI, StAR, parts of the OECD base-erosion work, but nothing on the table yet makes cooperation automatic or binding. The countervailing dangers: measurement, overreach and the politics of blame. Critics of broadening the “illicit” label reasonably warn about two dangers: first, measurement errors if you don’t separate price-driven trade variation from mis-invoicing, you risk over-estimating damage; second, politicization, a too-elastic definition of “illicit” could be used by illiberal governments to scapegoat outside actors for internal failure. The AU Secretariat acknowledges both pitfalls and responds with technical guardrails: clearer statistical standards, trusted third-party trade data reconciliation, and legal thresholds aimed at activity that is designed to conceal value or evade domestic obligations, not ordinary cross-border commerce. The debate over definitions is not academic: it will determine whether the world builds systems to protect public revenue or creates a new layer of geopolitical rancour. Voices from global leaders and institutions (direct quotes). The moral and political case is being made in public by key actors. The UN has repeatedly framed the drain on developing countries as a massive development obstacle: the UN Secretariat and senior officials have called for urgent action to recover stolen assets and to tighten global frameworks that allow corruption and illicit flows to prosper. The World Bank–UNODC StAR initiative has said bluntly that asset recovery “is possible, but it is only rarely done at scale,” a policy failure, not simply a technical challenge. Meanwhile, the AU report quotes AU officials and leaders urging a global coherence: “there is a need to establish a global coherence of what has been agreed by African and non-African countries on efforts to curtail IFFs,” the Secretariat records, underscoring the insistence that high-minded resolutions must become binding practice. ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27. Charts, data, and the visual story. Numbers can be used to hide as much as to reveal, which is why transparent, comparable figures matter. To help readers see scale, I’ve prepared comparative charts highlighting the ranges and single-channel shocks: (a) the AU Secretariat’s continental range for annual illicit outflows (tens of billions), (b) the Swissaid estimate for 2022 gold smuggling (~$30–31bn), (c) the Ghana-specific Reuters figure (~$11.4bn lost over recent years), and (d) older but still instructive GFI developing-country estimates (hundreds of billions). These charts are attached and available for download: they don’t answer every methodological question, but they make the arithmetic unavoidable and the political stakes visible. What would real global accountability look like, step by step? If policymakers were serious tomorrow, the sequence is straightforward and politically painful: (1) the UN General Assembly or Security Council endorses a binding set of standards that expand “illicit” to include systematic fiscal damage caused by tax abuse and trade mis-invoicing; (2) jurisdictions adopt automatic exchange of beneficial-ownership and trade-transaction data; (3) major commodity hubs commit to traceability standards for high-risk goods; (4) an international asset-recovery fast-track is established (special bench, regional investigators, agreed evidentiary standards); (5) repatriated funds are deposited into insulated, transparent development accounts with civil-society oversight. Each step is negotiable in detail but not optional in logic: return without protection invites recapture; reform without return looks like virtue signalling. The AU report insists both must proceed together. The world’s choice and the stakes for ordinary people. This isn’t a debate between wealthy philanthropists and impecunious states; it is a contest over whether the rules of the global economy will be structured to privilege private secrecy or public accountability. For people in low-income countries, the difference is brutal: an extra $30–$60 billion a year on the continent or even the selective return of tens of billions tied to criminal cases would alter schooling, health care, water systems, and public investment in ways aid never has. Absent that, governments borrow more, cut services, and the cycle of grievance that fuels violence and corruption deepens. The AU Secretariat’s message is urgent and blunt: structural reform is development policy. A final provocation: what if the problem were framed as theft by design? The AU report’s most uncomfortable claim is that current international law and practice crafted in eras that valued secrecy and capital mobility now function effectively as a permissive architecture for theft on a grand scale. Rewriting the rules will be politically fraught; it will require confronting banks, law firms, market intermediaries, and states that profit from opacity. But the alternative is simple and grim: continue the hemorrhage and accept the politics that follow. That is the stark choice the new AU stocktake places before the UN and the world.

item.title: MONEY ON THE RUN: the Secret Routes of the World’s Stolen Wealth
item.content:encoded: Ayele Addis Ambelu Journalist at Africa News Channel and Ethiopian Mass Media (EMMA NEWS) Media Educator at Bahir Dar University. ⓒ천지일보 The numbers read like an act of global looting: tens of billions of dollars siphoned out of fragile states every year, hidden behind shell companies, rushed through secretive commodity channels, cleaned by fast judges and polite banks in distant capitals, and, crucially, rarely returned. A fresh stocktake by the Secretariat of the African Union High-Level Panel on Illicit Financial Flows warns that the international legal and financial architecture that should stop these flows is instead a set of cracked doors and unlocked safes. The Secretariat bluntly finds that the rules, practices, and institutions that abroad jurisdictions rely on to freeze, trace, and repatriate illicit wealth systematically hamper recovery and that Africa, and many other developing regions, cannot continue to beg for crumbs when trillions in private wealth are at stake. This is a global problem, not an African parable. Global Financial Integrity’s influential estimates of trade-based illicit flows, historically used by researchers and policy makers, put the scale for developing countries in the hundreds of billions annually (earlier GFI estimates scaled at roughly $858–$1,060 billion for broader developing-country flows), a reminder that the problem is structural and transregional, not simply local theft. The AU’s own new analysis, while focused on the continent, explicitly ties African losses to patterns that happen, with variations, across Latin America, parts of Asia, and even inside advanced financial centers. How big is the leak? Different methods, different answers, and that’s the point. The AU Secretariat cites a continental annual hemorrhage in the tens of billions (it frames a plausible range used by continental analysts), and independent NGO research into one high-risk channel, artisanal gold, puts a single commodity’s annual leak at roughly the same order of magnitude. Swissaid’s 2024 field and trade-data study estimated at least $30–$35 billion of undeclared/illicit African gold exports in 2022 alone, much of it flowing through refining hubs in the UAE, Turkey, Switzerland, and India, where traceability evaporates after refining. In a single country case that reads like a razor to the national ledger, Reuters reported that Ghana alone may have lost about $11.4 billion to gold smuggling over a recent five-year span, enough to fund large chunks of national development programs or to substantially reduce sovereign borrowing. ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27. “Why should returns be treated like charity?” That indignation is not mine; it is the document’s logic. The AU Secretariat urges the UN and other global institutions to revise narrow legal definitions of “illicit” wealth to fold into the concept not only plainly criminal proceeds (embezzlement, drug profits, war-era looting) but also cross-border tax abuse, trade-misinvoicing, and aggressive profit-shifting that, while sometimes technically legal, amount to the systematic siphoning of public revenue. That conceptual shift would change the toolkit: from a reliance on slow, ad-hoc mutual legal assistance to routine, multilateral statistical monitoring, automatic sharing of beneficial-ownership data, and binding rules for fast asset freezes. In short, treat these flows as fiscal and development harms as much as criminal acts. There are voices at the top calling this what it is. United Nations institutions and global panels have repeatedly framed illicit flows as a development and security emergency: “Illicit financial flows already deprive developing countries of hundreds of billions of dollars every year,” the UN Secretariat has warned in multiple fora, and the FACTI Panel and UNODC have asked for joined-up reforms across tax, trade, and anti-money-laundering systems. The World Bank / UNODC Stolen Asset Recovery Initiative (StAR), the practitioner shop that works on the ground to pull stolen assets back, has for years highlighted how legal fragmentation and banking secrecy turn asset recovery into a trickle, not a river. The AU paper’s prescription echoes that chorus: return and reform must go hand in hand. Mechanisms of the global heist, how money leaves and why it vanishes? The playbook is now well known to anyone who studies global money flows, and the AU report lays it out with grim clarity: commercial channels (trade mis-invoicing and aggressive transfer-pricing), the informal commodity chain (artisanal minerals, timber, sometimes wildlife and fisheries), and the classic kleptocrat pathway (embezzlement routed through shell companies and luxury real estate). Each channel exploits a different legal or institutional gap: poor customs controls and weak regional border oversight for commodities; opaque corporate structures and lax country-by-country reporting for profit shifting; and secrecy jurisdictions and weak beneficial-ownership rules for kleptocratic flight. Because the beneficiaries of these systems are dispersed financiers, law firms, extraction companies, and private vaults in major cities, answering the crime requires cross-border rules that current institutions were not designed to deliver. A single case, global echoes: Ghana’s gold story. Ghana is a cautionary tale and a template. The Swissaid data and subsequent reporting show vast quantities of artisanal gold leaving West Africa under the radar, carried by passengers, misdeclared in trade reports, or routed through porous borders to hubs that absorb and refine gold beyond easy audit. Reuters’ in-depth reporting found that over recent years, Ghana lost an estimated $11.4 billion to smuggling and under-declaration — money that, in a basic arithmetic of governance, could pay for hospitals, schools, and roads. That loss is not just an accounting footnote; it weakens tax bases, increases borrowing, deepens inequality, and funds criminal and sometimes violent networks. But crucially, the route the gold takes through Dubai, Swiss vaults, and dozens of dealer networks is the same route by which other forms of wealth disappear from the books across continents. The global pattern is the same; the victims are many. Why the rich countries and financial hubs resist change and why that matters for everyone. The AU Secretariat’s stocktake is unambiguous: recovery is asymmetric. Courts and enforcement in wealthy jurisdictions sit at chokepoints. Freezing and repatriating assets requires cooperation and political will from the jurisdictions that host banks, real estate, and legal services used to hide money. That gives those jurisdictions leverage, sometimes leveraged into delay. The political economy is stark: opacity creates profit for banks and service providers, and the regulatory cost of full transparency looks like a business risk to powerful actors. This explains why international agreements remain patchy, why mutual legal assistance procedures are slow, and why Africa (and other claimants) often have to beg for cooperation instead of asserting a right enforced by a global mechanism. The AU report insists this asymmetric dependence must end: Africa must be empowered to trace and recover assets without relying on sporadic cooperation. The program for a global fix is bold, precise, and doable. The AU Secretariat and allied global panels not only diagnose, but they also provide a practical toolbox. The measures most likely to cut the leak include: automatic and reciprocal exchange of beneficial-ownership records; mandatory country-by-country corporate reporting and a clampdown on abusive transfer pricing; trade-data reconciliation programs that identify misinvoicing in near-real time; tighter controls on high-risk commodities with traceability through the supply chain; harmonized criteria for rapid asset freezes; and regional asset-recovery platforms underwritten by UN or regional institutions that speed repatriation while insulating returned funds from capture. Many of these reforms are already being piloted in bits and pieces, FACTI, StAR, parts of the OECD base-erosion work, but nothing on the table yet makes cooperation automatic or binding. The countervailing dangers: measurement, overreach and the politics of blame. Critics of broadening the “illicit” label reasonably warn about two dangers: first, measurement errors if you don’t separate price-driven trade variation from mis-invoicing, you risk over-estimating damage; second, politicization, a too-elastic definition of “illicit” could be used by illiberal governments to scapegoat outside actors for internal failure. The AU Secretariat acknowledges both pitfalls and responds with technical guardrails: clearer statistical standards, trusted third-party trade data reconciliation, and legal thresholds aimed at activity that is designed to conceal value or evade domestic obligations, not ordinary cross-border commerce. The debate over definitions is not academic: it will determine whether the world builds systems to protect public revenue or creates a new layer of geopolitical rancour. Voices from global leaders and institutions (direct quotes). The moral and political case is being made in public by key actors. The UN has repeatedly framed the drain on developing countries as a massive development obstacle: the UN Secretariat and senior officials have called for urgent action to recover stolen assets and to tighten global frameworks that allow corruption and illicit flows to prosper. The World Bank–UNODC StAR initiative has said bluntly that asset recovery “is possible, but it is only rarely done at scale,” a policy failure, not simply a technical challenge. Meanwhile, the AU report quotes AU officials and leaders urging a global coherence: “there is a need to establish a global coherence of what has been agreed by African and non-African countries on efforts to curtail IFFs,” the Secretariat records, underscoring the insistence that high-minded resolutions must become binding practice. ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27. Charts, data, and the visual story. Numbers can be used to hide as much as to reveal, which is why transparent, comparable figures matter. To help readers see scale, I’ve prepared comparative charts highlighting the ranges and single-channel shocks: (a) the AU Secretariat’s continental range for annual illicit outflows (tens of billions), (b) the Swissaid estimate for 2022 gold smuggling (~$30–31bn), (c) the Ghana-specific Reuters figure (~$11.4bn lost over recent years), and (d) older but still instructive GFI developing-country estimates (hundreds of billions). These charts are attached and available for download: they don’t answer every methodological question, but they make the arithmetic unavoidable and the political stakes visible. What would real global accountability look like, step by step? If policymakers were serious tomorrow, the sequence is straightforward and politically painful: (1) the UN General Assembly or Security Council endorses a binding set of standards that expand “illicit” to include systematic fiscal damage caused by tax abuse and trade mis-invoicing; (2) jurisdictions adopt automatic exchange of beneficial-ownership and trade-transaction data; (3) major commodity hubs commit to traceability standards for high-risk goods; (4) an international asset-recovery fast-track is established (special bench, regional investigators, agreed evidentiary standards); (5) repatriated funds are deposited into insulated, transparent development accounts with civil-society oversight. Each step is negotiable in detail but not optional in logic: return without protection invites recapture; reform without return looks like virtue signalling. The AU report insists both must proceed together. The world’s choice and the stakes for ordinary people. This isn’t a debate between wealthy philanthropists and impecunious states; it is a contest over whether the rules of the global economy will be structured to privilege private secrecy or public accountability. For people in low-income countries, the difference is brutal: an extra $30–$60 billion a year on the continent or even the selective return of tens of billions tied to criminal cases would alter schooling, health care, water systems, and public investment in ways aid never has. Absent that, governments borrow more, cut services, and the cycle of grievance that fuels violence and corruption deepens. The AU Secretariat’s message is urgent and blunt: structural reform is development policy. A final provocation: what if the problem were framed as theft by design? The AU report’s most uncomfortable claim is that current international law and practice crafted in eras that valued secrecy and capital mobility now function effectively as a permissive architecture for theft on a grand scale. Rewriting the rules will be politically fraught; it will require confronting banks, law firms, market intermediaries, and states that profit from opacity. But the alternative is simple and grim: continue the hemorrhage and accept the politics that follow. That is the stark choice the new AU stocktake places before the UN and the world.

item.title: 지구런, 대전현충원서 ‘보훈·환경 러닝’으로 달리며 기억하다
item.content:encoded: 국립대전현충원에서 열린 ‘지구런 현충원 환경봉사 & 보훈 챌린지’ 참가자들이 지난 25일 묘역 정화활동을 하고 있다. (제공: 지구런) ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27.   환경보전·보훈·건강 결합한 전국 첫 융합형 봉사 프로그램 [천지일보 대전=김지현 기자] 환경과 보훈의 가치를 함께 실천하는 러닝 캠페인 ‘지구런(GroundRun)’이 25일 국립대전현충원에서 ‘현충원 환경봉사 & 보훈 챌린지’를 개최했다. 이번 행사는 사단법인 대한참전유공자환경봉사단이 주최하고, 지구런이 주관했다. 슬로건은 “달리지 못할 길은 없다! 함께 달리며, 함께 기억하며, 함께 봉사합니다!”였다. 지구런은 단순한 달리기를 넘어 보훈(報勳)과 환경보전, 시민건강을 결합한 사회공헌형 러닝 프로젝트로, 전국 러너들이 ‘달리며 기억하는 봉사’를 실천하는 데 목적을 두고 있다. 이번 대전현충원 챌린지는 첫 사회공헌형 참여 프로그램으로, 순국선열과 호국영령의 숭고한 희생을 기리며 현충원 일대 환경정화 활동을 펼쳤다. 국립대전현충원에서 열린 ‘지구런 현충원 환경봉사 & 보훈 챌린지’ 참가자들이 지난 25일 참배길과 묘역 주변을 걷고 있다. (제공: 지구런) ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27. 참가자들은 참배길과 묘역 주변을 걸으며 약 4000기의 묘비를 정화하고 ‘기억과 실천의 길’을 달리며 보훈의 의미를 되새겼다. 특히 런포레멤버, 스탭포워드, 히어로즈환경봉사러닝, 러너즈 등 시민 러닝 크루가 자발적으로 참여해 세대와 세대를 잇는 새로운 시민봉사 모델을 만들어냈다. 지구런 관계자는 “이번 현충원 행사는 러너들이 달리기를 통해 환경과 기억, 그리고 감사의 마음을 표현하는 새로운 형태의 사회공헌 모델”이라며 “국가유공자에 대한 존경과 지구를 지키는 실천을 하나로 묶은 최초의 융합형 프로그램으로 전국 확산을 추진하겠다”고 밝혔다. 전병권 대한참전유공자환경봉사단 총재는 “지구런의 취지에 깊이 공감한다”며 “현충원을 방문할 때마다 느꼈던 감사와 환경관리의 중요성을 시민과 함께 실천할 수 있어 뜻깊었다. 앞으로 청소년과 참전유공자 세대가 함께하는 사회통합형 봉사문화로 발전시키겠다”고 말했다. 행사에 참여한 시민들은 “달리며 묘역을 정화하니 마음이 숙연해졌다”며 “젊은 세대와 참전유공자가 함께 국가를 위해 희생한 분들을 기억하고, 땀 흘리며 환경을 가꾸는 것이 진정한 보훈이라고 느꼈다”고 소감을 전했다. 지구런은 환경보전과 시민건강을 동시에 실천하는 ‘지속가능 러닝 플랫폼’으로, 봉사·기부형 챌린지를 전국 러너 네트워크와 함께 확산 중이다. 이번 대전현충원 프로그램을 시작으로, 앞으로도 지역사회·공공기관·시민이 함께 만드는 러닝 기반 사회공헌 생태계를 구축해 나갈 계획이다.

item.title: ‘병아리콩·햄프시드’로 만든 간편식… 삼양식품, 식물성 스낵 ‘펄스랩’ GS샵 첫 론칭
item.content:encoded: 삼양식품이 홈쇼핑을 통해 판매를 시작한 식물성 간편식 브랜드 ‘펄스랩’ 제품 4종. (제공: 삼양식품) ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27. [천지일보=양효선 기자] 삼양식품은 27일 자사 식물성 간편식 브랜드 ‘펄스랩(PULSE LAB)’ 제품을 처음으로 홈쇼핑 채널에서 판매한다고 27일 밝혔다. 이날 오후 5시 35분부터 1시간 동안 GS샵을 통해 생방송으로 진행된다. ‘펄스랩’은 콩류(pulse)와 실험실(laboratory)의 합성어로, 콩을 기반으로 한 다양한 실험을 통해 차별화된 스낵 간편식을 선보이겠다는 의미를 담았다. 지난 7월 브랜드를 론칭한 이후 홈쇼핑 채널 진출은 이번이 처음이다. 출시 제품은 총 4종이다. ‘한입 쏙! 후무스’ 캐슈넛, 핫스파이시, ‘한입 쏙! 식물성 너겟’ 스위트갈릭, 크러쉬드페퍼 등으로 삼양식품이 자체 개발한 식물성 단백질과 병아리콩을 사용해 단백질과 식이섬유 함량이 높은 것이 특징이다. 이번 방송에서는 각 제품 3팩씩 구성된 4종 세트를 홈쇼핑 최저가로 선보이며 구매 고객 중 일부를 추첨해 펄스랩 보냉백 굿즈와 삼양라면, 불닭소스 등 사은품도 증정한다. 제품은 별도 해동 없이 냉동 상태 그대로 전자레인지나 에어프라이어로 조리할 수 있어 간편한 식사를 원하는 1인 가구와 바쁜 가족 단위 소비자에게 큰 인기를 끌 것으로 기대된다. 삼양식품 관계자는 “최근 건강 간식과 식사 대용 스낵에 대한 수요가 늘고 있어 더 많은 소비자에게 펄스랩을 알리기 위해 홈쇼핑 판매를 기획했다”며 “앞으로도 다양한 식물성 스낵 제품을 지속 선보일 예정”이라고 말했다.

item.title: 100% 천연 펄프 경쟁… 깨끗한나라 ‘블랑크’·쌍용C&B ‘코디 코튼 소프트’ 동시 출격
item.content:encoded: 쌍용C&B의 신제품 ‘코디 코튼 소프트’. 지폭 107mm, 롤 길이 36m의 와이드·롱롤 설계로 사용 편의성과 경제성을 높였다. (제공: 쌍용C&B) ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27. [천지일보=양효선 기자] 패키징과 위생용품 산업에서 천연펄프를 활용한 프리미엄 제품 경쟁이 본격화되고 있다. 깨끗한나라와 쌍용C&B는 각각 고급 백판지와 화장지 신제품을 27일 일제히 선보이며 시장 공략에 나섰다.  생활 혁신 솔루션 기업 깨끗한나라는 이날 100% 천연 펄프로 제작한 프리미엄 백판지 브랜드 ‘블랑크(Blanq)’를 새롭게 출시했다고 밝혔다. 깨끗한나라는 기존의 산업용 수출 라인 ‘화이트 호스(White Horse)’와 친환경 리사이클 제품군 ‘엔투엔(N2N)’에 이어 이번 프리미엄 브랜드 출시로 “산업용·친환경·프리미엄을 아우르는 3대 브랜드 체계”를 완성하게 됐다고 설명했다. ‘블랑크(Blanq)’는 ‘자연의 순수함에 기술의 정교함을 더한 프리미엄 백판지’를 콘셉트로, 고백색·고평활 인쇄 품질과 3-Ply 다층 구조로 높은 강도와 원단 효율성을 구현한 것이 특징이다. 회사 측은 같은 평량에서도 더 두껍고 견고한 질감을 구현함으로써 생산성과 원가 경쟁력을 동시에 확보했다는 점도 강조했다. 라인업은 ▲‘Blanq-Cream’ ▲‘Blanq-HBP’ ▲‘Blanq-Light’ ▲‘Blanq-Bright’ 등 4종으로, 식품·화장품·전자·패션 산업 등 다양한 고부가가치 패키징 수요에 대응한다. 전 제품은 FSC 및 PEFC 산림관리 인증을 획득해 ‘자원 순환과 환경 보전을 함께 고려한 지속가능한 소재’로서 신뢰성을 확보했다고 회사 측은 전했다. 깨끗한나라 관계자는 “‘블랑크(Blanq)’는 깨끗한나라 PS사업부가 축적해 온 기술력과 품질 노하우를 기반으로, 변화하는 글로벌 패키징 시장의 프리미엄 트렌드를 선도하기 위해 기획된 브랜드”라며 “지속가능한 소재 혁신을 통해 산업 생태계의 발전 방향을 제시해 나가겠다”고 말했다. 깨끗한나라가 출시한 프리미엄 백판지 브랜드 ‘Blanq(블랑크)’. 100% 천연 펄프 기반으로 고백색·고평활 인쇄 품질을 구현했다. (제공: 깨끗한 나라) ⓒ천지일보 2025.10.27. 같은 날 생활위생 전문기업 쌍용C&B도 부드러움과 편의성을 높인 신제품 ‘코디 코튼 소프트’를 출시했다. ‘코디 코튼 소프트’는 ‘천연펄프 100% 무형광 제품’으로, 스페인산 천연 코튼(1000ppm)을 함유해 극강의 부드럽고 포근한 질감을 구현했다고 회사 측은 전했다. 피부에 직접 닿는 제품인 만큼 부드러움과 안전성을 모두 고려했다는 설명이다. 제품은 지폭 107mm로 기존 제품보다 약 9mm 넓고 롤 길이도 36m로 기존(30m)보다 약 20% 길어졌다. 이에 따라 ‘한 장으로도 충분한 사용감’을 제공하고 제품 구매 주기를 늘려 경제성도 높였다고 전했다. 신제품은 이달 말부터 전국 농협을 통해 공식 판매에 들어가며 프로모션도 병행될 예정이다. 쌍용C&B 관계자는 “‘코디 코튼 소프트’는 스페인산 코튼 함유에 기존 제품보다 넓고 길어 극강의 부드러움과 사용 편의성을 겸비한 제품으로, 소비자의 높은 만족을 이끌어 낼 수 있을 것으로 기대된다”라며 “앞으로도 품질 경쟁력을 강화하고 소비자 생활에 밀착한 제품 개발을 지속해 나가겠다”고 말했다.
